newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban's Afghan foes cement gains, threaten Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Taleban's Afghan foes cement gains, threaten Kabul.

text.p: Taleban fighters reinforced defences around the Afghan capital on Monday as their foes consolidated weekend advances and forged a political alliance with northern leader Abdul Rashid Dostum.
The fundamentalist Taleban, rulers of most of Afghanistan for the past two weeks, admitted losing towns on the road north of Kabul but vowed they would roll Masood's forces back.
Dostum, a powerful Uzbek warlord, recognised Afghanistan's ousted goverment on Monday, but held back from joining a military alliance with its forces around Kabul.

"We recognised Mr. (Burhanuddin) Rabbani's government," a spokesman for the northern leader, Abdul Rashid Dostum, told reporters after a five-hour-long meeting at the top of the Salang Pass north of Kabul.

"We (also) set up a commission today to consider the proper roles and responsibilities of the (Dostum forces) in the government as well as those of other parties," the spokesman, General Mohamed Youssef, added.

General Dostum, estranged from the Rabbani government and especially from Rabbani's Defence Minister, Ahmad Shah Masood, since 1994, has been much courted since Taleban forces drove the government out of Kabul little more than two weeks ago.

Dostum's recognition of Rabbani as the legitimate head of state during his second meeting with Masood in a week suggests a ring of hostile forces is being set in place around the mainly Pushtun Taleban, who now occupy about two-thirds of Afghanistan.
Dostum controls six provinces north of the Hindu Kush mountains and Afghan watchers say his support is key to any push by Masood and his political mentor Rabbani to recover power.
Masood's mainly ethnic Tajik fighters consolidated control of the two towns on the road from Kabul to the Salang, the strategically important Jabal os-Siraj and Charikar.
The gains leave him less than an hour's drive from Kabul.
Travellers and witnesses said sporadic fighting was still going on around Charikar.

A Masood spokesman said his forces had on Monday taken all but one tip of the airbase of Bagram. The Taleban said earlier it retained control of the base. Travellers said earlier Masood forces were operating around the perimeter and on nearby roads.
Earlier Dostum general Said Jasser Naderi held out the prospect of a peaceful takeover of the capital. "We want to take it (Kabul) by negotiation if possible, but if not..." he said.
Acting Taleban foreign minister Sher Mohammad Stanakzai told a news conference in Kabul earlier the Taleban was reinforcing the capital but doubted Masood had the strength to take it.

He rejected talks with Masood but reiterated the Taleban's readiness to talk to Dostum, provided he did not take up arms against it. Dostum aides in the Salang Pass said Dostum's support for Masood had so far been logistical.

"By now General Dostum must have realised that fighting has no use in our country so we request General Dostum that he should solve all the problems through negotiation, also through the United Nations," Stanakzai said earlier on Monday.

The Taleban's sweeping takeover of Kabul and nearby cities last month surprised many Afghans and convinced some Afghan watchers they could similarly overwhelm Masood's bruised forces in his Panjsher valley stronghold.

But in less than a week it has lost many of its gains in territory north of Kabul to Masood. Taleban sources have said the militia has suffered heavy casualties and lost one of its top commanders, Mullah Abdul Ahad, killed in fighting.
Stanakzai said the Taleban had suffered casualties and said some wounded were being shipped to the southern town of Kandahar, the Taleban's headquarters. He declined to give details.

Kabul was tense but quiet on Monday, apart from an outburst of firing across the capital for about an hour after nightfall. There was no immediate explanation for the firing, most of it anti-aircraft and small arms fire.
